content.title: KITCHEN MISTAKES THAT ARE QUIETLY MAKING YOUR {{FOOD}} DANGEROUS
facts: **Melon** – Leaving cut melon out at room temperature for hours (bacteria like Salmonella and Listeria multiply fast on its moist, low-acid flesh).
**Chicken** – Rinsing raw chicken under the tap before cooking (splashes spread Campylobacter and Salmonella across your sink, counters, and dishes).
**Potatoes** – Storing them in the fridge (cold temps convert starch to sugar, which can form more acrylamide when fried or roasted at high heat).
**Leftover pasta or rice** – Cooling it slowly on the counter for hours (Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and multiply as food sits warm).
**Eggs** – Storing them on the fridge door (temperature swings every time the door opens speed up bacterial growth and shorten shelf life).
**Garlic in oil** – Making a homemade garlic-oil infusion and leaving it unrefrigerated (low-oxygen environment lets Clostridium botulinum spores grow).
**Ground beef** – Judging doneness by color alone (only a food thermometer confirms it's hit a safe internal temperature, since browning can happen before bacteria are killed).
**Berries** – Washing them right after buying instead of right before eating (extra moisture sitting in the fridge speeds up mold growth).

content.caption:
Quick real talk on a few of these: cut **melon** is one of the riskiest fruits to leave out because its flesh has almost no acidity to slow bacteria down, so what starts as a small amount of Salmonella on the rind can spread through the fruit within hours at room temp. With **chicken**, rinsing feels like a hygiene habit, but water droplets can travel up to 3 feet from your sink, landing on sponges, towels, and countertops where they linger long after you've moved on. And that **garlic** in oil situation is sneaky — botulism spores don't need much oxygen to grow, and infused oil sitting on the counter is exactly the low-oxygen, room-temp environment they thrive in, even though everything still looks and smells fine. Everyone's kitchen habits are a little different, so it's worth double-checking your own routine against these.
